title: GSAcc: Accelerate 3D Gaussian Splatting via Depth Speculation and Gaussian-centric Rasterization
problem: GPU-based 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering suffers from insufficient parallelism in sequential pipeline stages and large memory overhead for intermediate results.
method: GSAcc introduces Gaussian depth speculation to parallelize preprocessing and sorting. A Gaussian-centric dataflow interleaves preprocessing and rasterization, executing all steps concurrently without storing intermediates. Dedicated hardware accelerates sorting and rasterization.

title: Towards Uncertainty-aware Robotic Perception via Mixed-signal BNN Engine Leveraging Probabilistic Quantum Tunneling
problem: Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) provide uncertainty quantification essential for safety-critical robotic perception, but traditional software BNNs have prohibitively high hardware overhead and latency, restricting real-time deployment on resource-constrained robots.
method: Mixed-signal hardware accelerator leverages probabilistic quantum tunneling in fully depleted silicon-on-insulator (FDSOI) transistors to generate Gaussian random variables efficiently (200 fJ/sample, r=0.997 correlation). Parallel BNN architecture uses this compact randomness source for low-latency probabilistic inference.

title: Local-GS: An Order-Independent Gaussian Splatting Training Accelerator Exploiting Splat Locality
problem: 3D Gaussian Splatting training on edge devices is bottlenecked by depth-wise data dependencies between overlapping Gaussians, limited memory, and hardware under-utilization. Order-dependent rendering requires sequential processing, preventing parallelism exploitation.
method: Local-GS introduces order-independent rendering to break depth-wise dependencies, enabling parallel pixel intersection test unit scheduling based on Gaussian splat locality. Unified training-rendering cores execute efficient splat-level parallel rendering and gradient propagation simultaneously, optimizing hardware utilization.

title: Unified Memory Protection with Multi-granular MAC and Integrity Tree for Heterogeneous Processors
problem: Hardware memory protection in heterogeneous SoCs (CPU + GPU + NPU) causes significant performance degradation because conventional fixed-granularity MACs and integrity trees are optimized for CPU access patterns but perform poorly under the diverse, irregular memory access patterns of GPUs and NPUs.
method: The authors propose a unified multi-granular MAC and integrity tree mechanism that supports four granularity levels for both MACs and counters. A multi-granular tree stores coarse-grained and fine-grained counters at different tree levels, and a dynamic detection mechanism selects the most appropriate granularity per memory region based on the observed access pattern from each processing unit. The design is further combined with prior sub-tree techniques to reduce tree traversal overhead.

title: BQSim: GPU-accelerated Batch Quantum Circuit Simulation using Decision Diagram
problem: Existing quantum circuit simulators process one input state at a time, but applications such as quantum testing and verification require simulating a circuit under multiple input states (batch simulation). No GPU-accelerated batch quantum circuit simulator exists that exploits shared structure across inputs.
method: BQSim uses decision diagrams (DDs) to compactly represent quantum gate matrices and identify shared structure across batch inputs, then converts the DD representation into a GPU-efficient data structure for parallel evaluation. A task-graph-based execution engine minimizes repetitive GPU kernel launch overhead by grouping related computations into batched kernel calls and overlapping kernel execution with data movement between host and device. The DD optimization step reduces the total computation needed for batch simulation by collapsing redundant operations shared across inputs.

title: Variational Quantum Algorithms in the era of Early Fault Tolerance
problem: Emerging 10,000-qubit devices with ~0.1% two-qubit error rates enable lightweight quantum error correction (QEC) but cannot afford the full qubit overhead of surface codes near threshold, leaving a regime—Early Fault Tolerance (EFT)—where error correction is partial and resource allocation strategy is unclear. Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs) must be adapted to exploit EFT resources efficiently without the hardware or qubit budget of full fault tolerance.
method: The work introduces partial QEC (pQEC) for VQAs in the EFT regime, which error-corrects Clifford operations using lightweight codes while performing non-Clifford (Rz) rotations via magic state injection rather than the more expensive T-state distillation. Architectural optimizations reduce circuit latency by 2x, and a qubit packing strategy achieves 66% qubit efficiency in the EFT regime. The approach is evaluated by comparing fidelity gains of pQEC-VQA against standard (uncorrected) VQA approaches across multiple EFT device parameter settings.

title: Easz: An Agile Transformer-based Image Compression Framework for Resource-constrained IoTs
problem: Neural image compression requires heavy encoder-decode structures and inflexible model-switching for different compression ratios, making deployment on edge IoT devices impractical due to computational and storage constraints.
method: Easz shifts computational overhead of encoding to server, avoiding heavy encode-decode on edge. Uses patch-erase algorithm with conditional uniform-based sampler to selectively remove image contents. Receiver reconstructs erased pixels via lightweight transformer-based framework. Adaptive across compression levels without model switching. Evaluated on real testbed.

title: GCStack+GCScaler: Fast and Accurate GPU Performance Analyses Using Fine-Grained Stall Cycle Accounting and Interval Analysis
problem: Existing GPU performance analysis tools use coarse-grained, issue-stage-centric, priority-based cycle stacks that exaggerate memory-side stalls, hide concurrent stall events, and require expensive cycle-level simulation repetition for each design variant.
method: GCStack captures all concurrently occurring stall events within each cycle and represents performance as a fine-grained cycle stack by attributing each stall cycle to all simultaneously active stall types rather than the single highest-priority one. GCScaler then uses interval analysis to analytically scale the fine-grained cycle stack from a baseline GPU to an alternative design point without re-simulation, applying separate analytical scaling models for idle and synchronization stalls. The combined method allows exploration of 1,000 GPU designs from a single simulation trace.

title: NetTAG: A Multimodal RTL-and-Layout-Aligned Netlist Foundation Model via Text-Attributed Graph
problem: Circuit representation learning methods rely on complex functional supervision (truth-table simulation) and handle only simple-and-inverter graphs, failing to encode diverse gate functionalities and lacking structural awareness needed for full netlist understanding.
method: NetTAG formulates netlists as text-attributed graphs with gates annotated by symbolic logic expressions and physical characteristics, combining an LLM-based text encoder for gate semantics and a graph transformer for structure; pre-trained with self-supervised objectives and aligned to RTL and layout stages.

title: ElasticMiter: Formally Verified Dataflow Circuit Rewrites
problem: Dataflow circuits produced by high-level synthesis (HLS) compilers cannot be optimized via standard sequential equivalence verification because their latency-insensitive handshake semantics are incompatible with traditional notions of sequential equivalence, leaving no sound basis for automated datapath simplification.
method: ElasticMiter develops a generic equivalence verification framework for latency-insensitive dataflow circuits by constructing a miter circuit that detects functional divergence under all possible token arrival patterns. It then defines a graph rewriting system over dataflow circuit DAGs where each rewrite rule is verified by the framework before being applied, guaranteeing the rewritten circuit is equivalent to the original. The approach handles elastic buffering, fork/join nodes, and control tokens that are absent in traditional sequential circuits.

title: Late Breaking Results: Customized Diffusion Model Empowered by Heterogeneous Graph Network for Effective Floorplanning
problem: Classical analytical floorplanners are sensitive to initial solution quality; learning-based methods suffer high computational complexity and inefficiency.
method: Proposes a customized diffusion model generating high-quality initial floorplans; integrates heterogeneous graph neural network (HGNN) to capture block-to-block and pin-to-block relationships; introduces guidance sampling function optimizing wirelength and overlap.

title: Late Breaking Results: Hybrid Logic Optimization with Predictive Self-Supervision
problem: Logic synthesis optimization methods are typically application-agnostic, but different circuit regions benefit from different optimization techniques; identifying optimal region-specific methods requires expensive simulation.
method: Extract subgraph-centered vertex features via local neighborhood analysis and optimization evaluation, propose a circuit partitioning method using these features to cluster circuits by compatibility with specific optimization methods, then merge cluster-optimized results; leverage self-supervised learning to predict vertex features efficiently.

title: Leveraging control-flow similarity to reduce branch predictor cold effects in microservices
problem: Microservices suffer from severe branch mispredictions due to cold branch predictor state when cores are shared across interleaved service invocations or power-gated between requests. This cold-start effect degrades tail latency under strict SLA constraints.
method: The authors propose Similarity-based Branch Prediction (SBP), a hybrid predictor that augments conventional history-based and static-hint predictors with a similarity component (CHESS). CHESS encodes the control flow of prior request executions into a compact reference execution trace, then identifies branches that are hard to predict via conventional means and redirects them to the similarity predictor. The similarity predictor leverages dynamic control-flow reconvergence analysis to replay past execution paths for matching current requests, requiring only 18.1 KB of additional storage.

title: Bit-slice Architecture for DNN Acceleration with Slice-level Sparsity Enhancement and Exploitation
problem: Existing bit-slice DNN accelerator architectures exploit sparsity only at coarse granularity — either input or weight sparsity independently — failing to simultaneously leverage both input and weight sparsity at fine (bit-slice chunk) granularity, leaving substantial computational savings unrealized.
method: BADA (Bit-slice Architecture for DNN Acceleration) introduces a front-end unit that generates bit-slices from operands and selectively gathers only non-zero slices using a packed-nonzero selection mechanism, forwarding them to a back-end signed MAC unit. The architecture skips computation for (a) bit-slice chunks containing all zeros (coarse-grained) and (b) any operand pair where either input or weight bit-slice is zero (fine-grained joint sparsity). Two algorithmic optimizations complement the hardware: (1) a novel 8-bit data bit-slice representation with no additional hardware overhead (vs. 6-7 bit limits in prior work); (2) a training-time weight distribution narrowing technique that increases the proportion of zero-valued higher-order bit-slices, enhancing slice-level weight sparsity.

title: ParGNN: A Scalable Graph Neural Network Training Framework on multi-GPUs
problem: Full-batch Graph Neural Network training on multi-GPU systems faces severe load imbalance and high communication overhead due to irregular graph structures and uneven vertex/edge distributions.
method: ParGNN employs profiler-guided adaptive load balancing with graph over-partitioning to mitigate load imbalance, plus a subgraph pipeline algorithm that overlaps computation and communication while maintaining training accuracy.

title: CIM-BLAS: Computing-in-Memory Accelerator for BLAS
problem: Basic Linear Algebra Subprograms (BLAS) are foundational for scientific/engineering computing but are data-intensive, bottlenecked by limited memory bandwidth in CPUs and GPUs. Memory bandwidth is the primary constraint for level-1/2 BLAS operations and a significant bottleneck for level-3 operations.
method: First CIM accelerator for BLAS based on non-volatile memory (NVM). Features unified floating-point pipeline supporting high-precision arithmetic (to handle BLAS variety). Configurable dataflows support diverse BLAS functions (levels 1, 2, 3). Memory-bound operations execute directly in memory; compute-bound ops leverage PIM's high parallelism.
